note: The argv->outcome conformance corpus both fake devpods are driven over.
There are two hand-written fake devpods in this repo -- an in-process one
(the Rust `DevpodMachine`) and a program that stands on PATH (the Python
`devpod_shim.py`) -- and they drifted, in the dangerous direction: one
refused `delete --ignore-not-found` where real devpod exits 0. A fake that
is STRICTER than the real tool fails runs that would have succeeded, and no
test of either fake against itself can see it. So the expectations live
here, once, and each fake is driven over every row by its own suite.
Every row's expected outcome is what REAL devpod v0.26.1 does, not what
either fake happens to do. `verified` says how that was established, per
row, and says so plainly where it could not be: a row measured against the
real binary and a row inherited from the two fakes agreeing are different
kinds of claim, and collapsing them is how the drift got in.
A row is: `given` (the workspaces the machine starts with), `argv` (what is
passed after `devpod`), `exit` (the expected exit code), and `then` (every
workspace that must exist afterwards, with its state, ordered by id).
stdout is deliberately NOT part of a row. Real devpod's own output here is
a timestamped, colourised log line (`16:28:03 done deleted workspace
delete.go:101`) that no fake reproduces and no caller in this repo parses.
Pinning text would pin a fake's invention; exit code and state effect are
the contract the code under test actually depends on. Where output shape
does matter -- `list --output json` carrying no state field, `provider list
--output json` being an object keyed by name -- each fake's own tests pin
it against the recorded fixtures beside this file.

rows.name: delete of a missing workspace with --ignore-not-found succeeds
rows.why: The drift that motivated the corpus. `dl <ws> rm --force` passes this flag on every forced remove, so a fake that refuses fails a run real devpod completes.
rows.verified: measured: real devpod v0.26.1 on the host exits 0 (printing its usual `done deleted workspace` log line).

rows.name: --ignore-not-found is honoured before the workspace too
rows.why: Real devpod is a cobra program and parses flags on either side of the positional; a fake that only looks at trailing argv would pass the row above and fail this one.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod delete --ignore-not-found ghost` at v0.26.1 exits 0.

rows.name: delete of a missing workspace without the flag refuses
rows.why: The flag is the whole difference; without it the refusal is correct and a fake that always succeeded would hide a real failure.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod delete ghost` at v0.26.1 exits 1 with `fatal workspace ghost not found`.

rows.name: delete removes the workspace it was given
rows.why: The ordinary path, so the flag rows above are not the only thing holding delete's shape.
rows.verified: unverified against the real binary: observing it needs a provisioned workspace and a container runtime. Inherited from `devpod delete --help` ("Deletes an existing workspace") and from both fakes agreeing.

rows.name: --ignore-not-found still deletes a workspace that is there
rows.why: The flag changes the missing case only. A fake that read it as "do nothing" would leave a workspace `dl <ws> rm --force` reported as removed.
rows.verified: unverified against the real binary for the same reason as the row above; `devpod delete --help` scopes the flag to "Treat 'workspace not found' as a successful delete".

rows.name: stop of a missing workspace refuses
rows.why: `stop` takes no flags at all at v0.26.1, so there is nothing here that could make it forgiving.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod stop ghost` at v0.26.1 exits 1 with `fatal workspace not found for args: [ghost]`.

rows.name: stop stops a running workspace
rows.why: The state effect `dl <ws> stop` depends on.
rows.verified: unverified against the real binary: needs a provisioned workspace. Inherited from `devpod stop --help` and both fakes agreeing.

rows.name: up in the order dl sends it, with every flag production passes
rows.why: The whole `devpod up` argv `dl` really builds, in its real order. Pins that no flag in it is mistaken for the workspace source.
rows.verified: measured for arity: `devpod up --help` at v0.26.1 gives every flag here a value (`--init-env`, `--mount` and `--dotfiles-script-env` are stringArray; `--workspace-env-file` and `--prebuild-repository` are strings; `--id`, `--ide`, `--devcontainer-path`, `--dotfiles` and `--dotfiles-script` are strings).

rows.name: up derives the id from the source with every production flag trailing it
rows.why: Same argv without `--id`, so the derived id is the observable. A value flag read as bare would push its value into the positionals, and with no `--id` to override it the derived id is what moves.
rows.verified: measured for arity, as the row above.

rows.name: up takes the positional source with --init-env in front of it
rows.why: The shape that turns the value-flag gap from latent into visible: read as bare, `--init-env` leaves `DL_WORKSPACE_ID=...` as the first positional and the fake creates a workspace named after an environment variable.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod up --init-env FOO=bar --mount type=bind,... /tmp/nope-xyz-123` at v0.26.1 reached the clone step for `/tmp/nope-xyz-123`, so the positional was the source and `FOO=bar` was never mistaken for one.

rows.name: up takes the positional source with --mount in front of it
rows.why: Same gap, the pixi-cache flag. Its value ends in `target=/opt/pixi-cache`, so a fake that mis-parses it names the workspace after the mount target.
rows.verified: measured, as the row above.

rows.name: up takes the positional source with --dotfiles-script in front of it
rows.why: Neither fake listed `--dotfiles-script`; both listed `--dotfiles`, which is a different flag with its own value.
rows.verified: measured for arity (`--dotfiles-script string`); interspersal measured on `up` as above.

rows.name: up takes the positional source with --dotfiles-script-env in front of it
rows.why: The third pixi-cache flag, and not a duplicate of `--workspace-env`: devpod gives the dotfiles install script an environment of its own.
rows.verified: measured for arity (`--dotfiles-script-env strings`); interspersal measured on `up` as above.

rows.name: up takes the positional source with --workspace-env-file in front of it
rows.why: How the host's GitHub token reaches a workspace, so this flag is on every launch that has a token to forward.
rows.verified: measured for arity (`--workspace-env-file strings`); interspersal measured on `up` as above.

rows.name: up restarts a stopped workspace addressed by its id
rows.why: `dl <ws> up` on an existing workspace hands devpod the id, not a path, and expects it running afterwards.
rows.verified: unverified against the real binary: needs a provisioned workspace. Inherited from `devpod up --help` (the positional is `[workspace-path|workspace-name]`) and both fakes agreeing.

rows.name: ssh with a trailing --workdir starts a stopped workspace
rows.why: The transport `dl` attaches with. A stopped workspace must come back running without an `up` of its own.
rows.verified: measured for arity (`--workdir string`). The start-on-ssh effect is unverified against the real binary -- it needs a provisioned workspace -- and is inherited from both fakes agreeing.

rows.name: ssh takes the positional workspace with --workdir in front of it
rows.why: A fake that reads `--workdir` as bare takes the directory as the workspace name and refuses a workspace that is there -- the same stricter-than-real failure as the delete row, on the attach path.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod ssh --workdir /w ghost` at v0.26.1 refuses with `workspace not found for args: [ghost]`, naming the positional and not the workdir, so the flag consumed its value. The start-on-ssh effect is inherited, as the row above.

rows.name: ssh with a workdir and a remote command runs against a running workspace
rows.why: The full attach argv, `--command` payload included, on the workspace state `dl` usually finds.
rows.verified: measured for arity (`--command string`, `--workdir string`).

rows.name: ssh into a workspace devpod never heard of refuses
rows.why: The honest non-zero exit; a fake that succeeded here would let a launch look like it attached to nothing.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod ssh ghost --workdir /w` at v0.26.1 exits 1.

rows.name: status of a missing workspace refuses
rows.why: How `dl` tells "stopped" from "never existed"; a zero exit here would collapse the two.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod status nosuchws --output json` at v0.26.1 exits 1 with `fatal workspace not found for args: [nosuchws]`.

rows.name: status reads a workspace without disturbing it
rows.why: A read must not start anything -- unlike ssh, which does.
rows.verified: unverified against the real binary: needs a provisioned workspace. Inherited from `devpod status --help` and both fakes agreeing.

rows.name: list on a machine with no workspaces succeeds
rows.why: An empty host is the first thing `dl` meets, and it is not an error.
rows.verified: measured: `devpod list --output json` against a fresh devpod home at v0.26.1 prints `[]` and exits 0.

rows.name: list leaves every workspace as it found it
rows.why: Same read-only claim as status, across the whole machine.
rows.verified: measured for exit and emptiness on a fresh home; the no-side-effects claim is inherited from `devpod list --help` and both fakes agreeing.

rows.name: a command devpod does not have refuses
rows.why: The fakes stand in front of the real CLI, and a typo'd verb must fail rather than quietly succeed.
rows.verified: measured for the class: cobra exits 1 on an unknown subcommand at v0.26.1.
